chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Once occasion noise is visible, the book widens to a collective setting. The chapter title points to a harder possibility than many people expect: groups can amplify noise.

That move matters because adding more people does not automatically smooth variation away. A committee or panel can intensify some drift instead of canceling it. The chapter extends the analysis of noise into group judgment rather than treating the group as a built-in cure.

This is where the warning matters. More voices change the process, but not always in the direction of steadier judgment. Collective interaction can make the spread louder instead of averaging the differences out.

The chapter keeps one useful limit in place. Group amplification is not a blanket case against all collective judgment, and it does not replace every other source of variation. The point is narrower and more practical. Groups have their own noise risks, and more people is not a simple cure.

That is what makes the chapter important after occasion noise. It shows that widening from one judge to many judges does not automatically solve the variation problem.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The chapter turns from occasion-level variation to group judgment. It argues that groups do not automatically reduce noise simply by involving more people.

That matters because a collective process can intensify variation instead of canceling it. The book wants that possibility taken seriously rather than hidden behind the comforting idea that more opinions always help.

This is the distinction it has to hold. Group amplification is a real risk, but it is not a reason to condemn all group judgment. The chapter is adding another layer to the analysis of spread, not replacing the rest of the picture with anti-group rhetoric.

The chapter keeps the limit visible. More people is not a simple cure, but neither is every committee automatically worse. It is claiming something narrower: collective processes have their own ways of generating or worsening noise.

That prepares the next move. Once group amplification is visible, the book can turn toward noise in predictive judgments.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The chapter takes away the easy comfort that more people mean less noise. It asks what happens when the room makes the wobble louder.

That matters because a committee can intensify drift instead of averaging it away, and the book wants that possibility dragged into the light. More voices do not automatically add up to cleaner judgment.

This is where the chapter gets sharper. Group amplification is not just another complaint about meetings. It is a real collective risk, but the chapter also refuses the lazy move of turning that into a blanket anti-group sermon.

The discipline stays narrow on purpose. No universal law is being offered here, and no one is saying every group is doomed. The chapter argues for a tougher account of collective judgment, not for a slogan.

That is what earns the next step. If the room can make noise louder, the next chapter can ask how predictive judgment carries its own noise problems.
